Content:
Let's recall the formula relating distance to speed and time:

Content:
[MATH: \text{speed} \times \text{time} = \text{distance}]

Content:
Using the relationship between multiplication and division, we can write this equation as

Content:
[MATH: \text{time} = \text{distance} \div \text{speed}]

Content:
which is equivalent to the formula

Content:
[MATH: \text{time} = \dfrac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}.]

Content:
We can use this formula to calculate the time taken for an object moving at a particular speed to cover a certain distance.

Content:
For example, suppose a plane flew for [MATH: 3\,120] kilometers at a constant speed of [MATH: 520] kilometers per hour. For how long was the plane in motion?

Content:
To determine the time the plane was in motion, we divide the distance, [MATH: 3\,120] kilometers, by the speed, [MATH: 520] kilometers per hour. This gives

Content:
[MATH: time|= (distance)/(speed); = (3120)/(520); = (3120 ÷ 10)/(520 ÷ 10); = (312)/(52); = 312 ÷ 52; = 6.]

Content:
Therefore, the plane was in motion for [MATH: 6] hours.
